notable_absence.finding: This page enumerates ten index kinds - primary, named primary, secondary, composite secondary, functional, array, partial, duplicate, covering, hyperscale vector, composite vector - and never once uses the words 'Traditional' or 'Vector' as classes, so the registry's promoted index-class:traditional / index-class:vector axis has no instance here despite the page being the natural place for it. Two further absences. (1) No relation could be extracted for the sentence 'It's not recommended to use primary keys for your production queries.' The section is about primary INDEXES and this sentence says primary KEYS - a different thing entirely (a key is data, an index is an artefact) - so the only faithful readings are either a defect or a claim about keys on a page about indexes. Omitted rather than guessed; see cross_component_finding. (2) The page has no requiresPrivilege, requiresServerRole or requiresCapellaRole relation at all: it shows a dozen CREATE INDEX statements and never says what access is needed to run one, unlike query-without-index.md in this same batch, which does.

cross_component_finding: Five things this page says that other parts of the corpus contradict or do not know. (1) 'It's not recommended to use primary keys for your production queries' - the section is Primary Index and the surrounding sentences are about the index; 'primary keys' is either a slip for 'primary indexes' or an SQL-ism imported wholesale. Either way a reader is told not to use something the same section has just told them to use. (2) index:index-partitioning versus n1ql:index-partitioning: the corpus's dominant spelling is n1ql: (11 files, including cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/index-partitioning.json), but round 16's namespace rule puts an index mechanic in index: and reserves n1ql: for statements, clauses and functions. Both spellings now exist and phase 2 must pick one; the SQL++ PARTITION BY HASH clause is legitimately n1ql:, the mechanism is not. (3) The Duplicate Index section says duplicate indexes give 'scale-out, Multi-Dimensional Scaling, performance, and high availability' - MDS is a node-placement architecture, and calling a round-robin over identical indexes 'Multi-Dimensional Scaling' stretches the promoted server:multi-dimensional-scaling concept past its own definition. (4) The page states the same key-type list twice, once per section ('scalar, object, or array' / 'a scalar field, object, or an array'), with different wording, instead of once. (5) The 'Examples on this Page' preamble (travel-sample plus set-the-query-context) is duplicated verbatim on index-replication.md and, in part, on query-without-index.md - three of the six pages in this batch carry the same boilerplate.
cross_product_finding: The registry glosses server:keyspace as 'the term the server/ tree uses where the Capella tree says collection'. This Capella page falsifies that: it says 'keyspace' fifteen times and 'collection' not once ('an index on the document key for the entire keyspace', 'any field within the keyspace', 'Couchbase keyspaces can have documents of various types'). index-lifecycle.md, three files away in the same Capella directory, does the opposite and says 'collection' throughout. So the keyspace/collection split is not a tree-level dialect difference as the registry records it; it varies page by page inside the Capella tree, and capella:collection and server:keyspace are both in live use for the same referent on adjacent pages. Separately, this page's structure is a near clone of server/7.2/learn/services-and-indexes/indexes/indexing-and-query-perf.md - same section order, same index kinds, same travel-sample examples - which is why every one of the six index-kind ids here already existed in the corpus at the extraction layer from that page. The two trees are maintaining one document twice.
